title: Verdant Systems - p95/p99 Latency Deep Dive
topics: VPC/on-prem network hops and LB behavior
summary: SE-led deep dive on tail latency drivers for Verdant's conversational product. Reviewed KV cache warmup, batching parameters, network hops from VPC egress, and quantization tradeoffs. Agreed to run controlled benchmarks with pinned model variants, cache warmers, and reduced tail batch sizes. Next steps include sharing benchmark sheet and scheduling an on-prem network trace session.
next_steps: Jenna Park - share Redwood benchmark spreadsheet + current config template - 2026-08-21
Marco Diaz - propose batching/cache config (warmup script & TTL settings) - 2026-08-24
Priya Raman/Samir Patel - run baseline p95/p99 on staging with 1k synthetic sessions and attach logs - 2026-08-28
Ivy Chen - schedule on-prem network trace session with Verdant networking team - 2026-08-25
action_items: Marco Diaz - build a KV cache warmer script and share example - 2026-08-24
Jenna Park - upload security/compliance pointer doc for VPC routing questions - 2026-08-21
Verdant (Priya) - export a sample edge-to-backend trace for 50 slow sessions - 2026-08-26
questions: How much of the p99 is network vs runtime?
Does streaming reduce observed p99 for multi-token outputs?
What cache TTL and eviction policy is Redwood recommending for variable-length convo workloads?
transcript:
[00:00] Jenna Park: Hi everyone, thanks for joining. we're gonna focus on p95/p99 tail today and dig into what you're seeing in production. Can everyone hear me?
[00:06] Alex Martinez: Yeah loud and clear. thanks.
[00:09] Priya Raman: yep, we can hear.
[00:12] Marco Diaz: Cool, i'll share my screen in a sec, got a few graphs to show.
[00:21] Samir Patel: Quick context - Verdant runs a conversational assistant with a mix of short queries and longer follow ups, we see good median latency ~80ms but p99 spikes to >1.2s under certain loads.
[00:33] Marco Diaz: Thanks, that's useful. first question - are you on hosted or dedicated?
[00:37] Priya Raman: We're on Redwood Dedicated, reserved capacity. GPUs are A100-ish in our cluster, but some of our traffic routes through a VPC peering link to the customer network (we're multi-tenant inside the VPC).
[00:48] Ivy Chen: ok. can you describe the typical request shape, token lengths?
[00:52] Priya Raman: 60% under 64 tokens, 30% 64-256, 10% >256. Key thing: we have bursts from batch uploads and also streaming clients.
[01:02] Marco Diaz: Got it. one obvious tail cause is cold KV cache for long contexts; another is batching jitter when long sequences cause variable per-token compute.
[01:12] Karen Liu: we also saw some network variance, internal LB + NATing through the VPC, sometimes extra hops on our side.
[01:20] Marco Diaz: can i show a p99 breakdown? (screen) so here's a sample: breakdown by component - network, queuing, runtime, tokenization. you can see in this run network is 30% of p99 but runtime is still significant.
[01:34] Alex Martinez: hmm, that matches our prometheus traces, but we wondered if streaming would mask some of the tail since you flush early.
[01:41] Marco Diaz: streaming helps perceived latency for the user because bytes arrive earlier, but end-to-end p99 for request completion can still be high if final steps (e.g., cache miss + large decode) happen. streaming splits perception vs completion.
[01:55] Priya Raman: curious about KV cache warmup. sometimes first few tokens are slow then subsequent messages are fast. what's the best practice?
[02:02] Marco Diaz: warm the KV cache by replaying prefixes you expect; Redwood supports a cache warmer script and keeping a TTL that survives typical convo gaps. also pinning model layers and using quantized checkpoints that are kernel-friendly reduces cold-run overhead.
[02:17] Samir Patel: we've tried a TTL of 300s but saw evictions during surges. does Redwood have advice on eviction policies?
[02:23] Ivy Chen: we recommend LRU with a conservative TTL for small working sets; if you have very large contexts consider sharding sessions across pods so the working set fits. also continuous batching is helpful - it groups requests without adding extra latency when tuned correctly.
[02:36] Alex Martinez: what about batching size? we tried auto-batching and noticed p99 increased during bursts.
[02:42] Marco Diaz: bigger batches improve throughput but can increase tail for latency-sensitive requests. we suggest a hybrid: small max batch for routed low-latency traffic and separate pools for high-throughput background workloads. Redwood routing can send low-latency traffic to dedicated lanes.
[02:56] Priya Raman: quantization - we have MLP concerns about accuracy. is int8 safe for our use case?
[03:01] Marco Diaz: quantization helps latency/throughput but may affect generation quality. we usually test int8 on a held-out eval set; for many transformer models int8 with per-channel scaling is within acceptable delta. if quality-sensitive, use int8 for embedding and non-critical endpoints, or mixed precision for the main model.
[03:18] Karen Liu: networking: our infra team flagged VPC egress NAT causing slow DNS and extra 20-40ms sometimes. could that explain p99?
[03:26] Marco Diaz: absolutely. network hops, NAT, cross-AZ routing can add variable latency. instrument packet trace from your VPC to Redwood endpoints. we also recommend keeping regional proximity and enabling private peering where possible to reduce NAT.
[03:41] Alex Martinez: any quick things we can flip?
[03:44] Marco Diaz: yes - lower max batch, enable KV cache warmer, increase cache TTL slightly, and test streaming mode for the client that cares about perceived latency. also add client-side retries with jitter instead of synchronous blocking calls.
[03:58] Priya Raman: on streaming, do you see cases where streaming increases p99?
[04:02] Marco Diaz: in some cases if the pipeline flushes in small chunks it reduces per-chunk latency but can increase compute overhead and scheduling churn on the pod, which could raise p99 under extreme concurrency. it's workload dependent.
[04:15] Samir Patel: can you walk through an example trace? our team uploaded two slow sessions earlier.
[04:20] Ivy Chen: sure, we pulled one of your slow traces - show time stamps: request enters edge -> LB -> NAT -> firewall -> Redwood ingress -> scheduler -> runtime -> model decode -> send. look at the spikes at scheduler + runtime for those ones.
[04:36] Priya Raman: i see a 300ms wait in scheduler for one session. what causes scheduler wait?
[04:40] Marco Diaz: scheduler wait can be batching alignment or waiting for dependent KV cache fetches. if many requests are competing for KV cache warmups they serialize. also small GC pauses on the worker process sometimes show up as microspikes.
[04:53] Alex Martinez: how do we isolate GC vs kernel inefficiencies?
[04:56] Marco Diaz: collect runtime traces & flamegraphs. Redwood can run a profiler on a test pod to show stalls. we can also attach a heap/GC trace.
[05:05] Karen Liu: what's the recommended experiment plan to measure improvement?
[05:08] Marco Diaz: 1) baseline run with current config (1k synthetic sessions) capturing p50/p95/p99 and traces, 2) add cache warmer & extended TTL, 3) reduce max batch for low-latency lane, 4) try streaming variant, 5) run quantized model if quality acceptable. each step isolate variables.
[05:26] Priya Raman: that sounds good. one more: we have private deployment (on-prem) tests coming up; any special networking gotchas?
[05:33] Marco Diaz: on-prem you need to watch NIC/PCIe saturation, NUMA affinity, and switch-level buffering. also ensure your private control plane for Redwood has proper routing so model downloads and metrics don't traverse slow paths. often tail spikes are due to ephemeral disk IO during model load if model is not fully pinned in memory.
[05:52] Samir Patel: model load spikes are interesting - we do see rare 2-3s stalls when a new variant loads after autoscale.
[05:58] Ivy Chen: reduce scale-in frequency or pre-warm new instances. preload quantized checkpoints into memory and avoid swap. set instance cold-start thresholds.
[06:10] Alex Martinez: is there a way to prioritize traffic in Redwood so our low-latency customers get smaller batches?
[06:15] Marco Diaz: yes, route by policy; you can tag low-latency requests and send them to a dedicated lane with low max-batch. Redwood console supports route-level throttle and lane assignment.
[06:26] Priya Raman: any concern about cost for separate lanes?
[06:29] Marco Diaz: there is a tradeoff; dedicated lanes cost more per qps but lower tail and better SLOs. Redwood Optimize can estimate unit economics for different configurations.
[06:42] Samir Patel: can you share examples of caching parameters others used?
[06:46] Marco Diaz: some customers use 10-15 minute TTL for conversational workloads with active users, LRU eviction, and a small persistent warming pool that holds hottest prefixes. others use per-session sharding to avoid cross-session eviction churn.
[06:58] Priya Raman: we want to test an LRU with 600s TTL and a 2-3 pod warming pool.
[07:04] Jenna Park: noted, we'll share example configs.
[07:07] Alex Martinez: about quantization again - what's the best way to validate quality quickly?
[07:11] Marco Diaz: run a small eval set of production prompts and compare metrics (ROUGE/BLEU or human eval for quality). Redwood can run an automated delta test against your baseline.
[07:22] Karen Liu: on the network side we'll run traceroutes for the slow sessions and collect tcpdump if needed.
[07:28] Marco Diaz: perfect. after that we can do a joint troubleshooting session with your SREs.
[07:33] Priya Raman: ok, timeline - we'll run baseline and collect traces by Aug 26.
[07:38] Jenna Park: i'll send the spreadsheet and config template by Aug 21. Marco will drop the cache warmer by Aug 24.
[07:44] Samir Patel: can we get a recommended max-batch number as a starting point?
[07:48] Marco Diaz: for low-latency lane start with max-batch 4-8 depending on model; observe p95/p99 tradeoffs.
[07:55] Alex Martinez: any notes on monitoring to catch tail early?
[07:58] Ivy Chen: alert on p95/p99 increase plus increase in scheduler wait time. also add trace sampling for any request > 2x median.
[08:08] Priya Raman: one last quick question - do you support cache persistence across restarts?
[08:12] Marco Diaz: currently KV cache is in-memory per pod; long-term persistence is on roadmap but can be approximated with pre-warming and sticky routing.
[08:22] Jenna Park: ok thanks everyone. we'll recap in email and include the spreadsheet + configs.
[08:27] Alex Martinez: appreciate it. talk soon.
[52:00] Meeting ends
file_notes: Transcript contains typical ASR artifacts: speaker labels occasionally generic, minor mis-recognitions (e.g., 'KV' as 'k v'), and some run-on sentences. References to config files and benchmark spreadsheet are placeholders for shared links Jenna will send.
